concept.name: Likelihood function
concept.definition: The joint probability (density) of the observed data expressed as a function of the model parameters with the data held fixed, L(theta) = f(y_1,...,y_n; theta). It measures the relative plausibility of parameter values and is the object maximized in maximum likelihood estimation, introduced by Fisher (1922).
concept.intuition: The same formula as the probability of the data, read backwards: instead of asking what data these parameters might produce, ask how probable this dataset is under each candidate parameter.
concept.mechanics: For i.i.d. data L(theta) = prod f(y_i; theta), and the log-likelihood l(theta) = sum log f(y_i; theta) is used for numerical stability. The score (gradient of l) and the Fisher information (expected negative curvature) drive estimation and inference, and likelihood ratios compare nested models.
concept.formula: L(theta) = prod_{i=1}^n f(y_i; theta); l(theta) = sum_i log f(y_i; theta); the likelihood ratio for two values is L(theta_1)/L(theta_2).
concept.failure_modes: The likelihood is only as meaningful as the assumed data-generating density; misspecification yields confident but wrong inference. Flat or ridged likelihoods indicate weak identification, and the likelihood alone carries no prior weighting.
concept.misconceptions: That the likelihood is a probability distribution over parameters: it is not normalized in theta and cannot be integrated as a probability without a prior.
concept.example: For ten independent Bernoulli trials with 7 successes, L(p) = p^7 (1-p)^3 is maximized at p = 0.7, so values near 0.7 are more likely explanations of the data than p = 0.5.
